classification.difficultyReason: Use the taught calculator method to approximate each root, compare the decimals and translate their order into number-line positions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 explicitly references Example 1 and assesses approximate placement of irrational numbers, rather than surd simplification. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 approximates each irrational number using a calculator to two decimal places, then locates the exact radical labels on a number line. Pages 3–6 provide the surrounding surd definitions and arithmetic methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the calculator approximation and number-line method demonstrated in Example 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a perfect-square factor and extract its square root, recognising when the entire radicand is a perfect square. Larger radicands require the same procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All twenty parts directly apply the basic surd results to a single square root; no distribution or rationalisation is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Extract perfect-square factors using the square-root product rule, as in Examples 2 and 3 on PDF page 4. Perfect squares use the positive square root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square-factor extraction to individual square roots, including two perfect squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a square factor, extract it and multiply by the existing coefficient; the perfect-square case leaves an integer.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts directly assess the basic surd results through square-factor extraction. Part j has a perfect-square radicand and simplifies to an integer. The provided reuse candidates have different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-root product rule to extract a perfect-square factor, then multiply its square root by the supplied coefficient. Example 3 on PDF page 4 explicitly demonstrates this method for multiples of surds; page 6 summarises square-factor extraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square-factor extraction and multiply by an existing integer coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught reverse extraction rule by squaring the positive coefficient and multiplying it into the radicand.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies the basic surd product result in reverse; no surd addition, expansion or rationalisation is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 on PDF page 5 reverses square-factor extraction: replace the positive coefficient by its square root, combine the factors under one radical and evaluate the whole-number radicand.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the square-root product rule in reverse, as demonstrated in Example 4.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply two square roots and remove any resulting perfect-square factor.

questions.mappingNote: Part a gives √6; b gives √77; c gives √40 and requires extracting 4; d gives √39; e gives √48 and requires extracting 16. Multiplication followed by simplification is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the product rule for positive square roots, then extract perfect-square factors. Example 5 on PDF page 5 demonstrates this sequence; PDF pages 3–4 explain square-factor simplification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply two square roots and remove any resulting perfect-square factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the quotient rule for square roots, with square-factor simplification in part f.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses the basic surd quotient result; part f additionally requires square-factor extraction. The source margin reference is Example 6.
questions.methodNote: Apply the square-root quotient rule as demonstrated in Example 6 on PDF page 5. For part f, remove the perfect-square factor from 8 using the simplification method on PDF pages 3–4.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the quotient rule for square roots, with square-factor simplification in part f.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine square-root multiplication, division and powers, then simplify perfect-square factors.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c and g use the product rule; e and h use the quotient rule; d and f use the square/root inverse results. Simplification in b–d and g–h uses perfect-square factors. The operations skill is the closest overall match.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes square-root product and quotient rules and inverse squaring/root operations. Page 4 extracts perfect-square factors. Page 5 Examples 5 and 6 demonstrate multiplying and dividing surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine square-root multiplication, division and powers, then simplify perfect-square factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Work backwards through root products and quotients to find missing factors, including interpreting the integer 2 as a square root in the final completion.

questions.mappingNote: Each part completes a square-root product or quotient directly using these rules, so surd-results is the closest assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states the product and quotient rules for square roots; page 5 Examples 5 and 6 demonstrate their application. Page 4 establishes exact surd form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete products and quotients using basic square-root rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply area formulas and inverse square-area calculations with exact surd lengths.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b apply the square-root product rule, c applies the square-root square identity, and d–e use positive square roots, with perfect-square extraction in e. The surd-results skill captures the shared assessed surd operations; secondary skills identify the geometric prerequisites.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes multiplication of square roots and the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots. Pages 4–5 demonstrate extracting perfect-square factors and retaining exact surd answers. The supplied pages do not establish the required area formulas or inverse area method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply area formulas and inverse square-area calculations with exact surd lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify hypotenuses and shorter sides, apply Pythagoras’ theorem and simplify exact square roots.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, c and e find hypotenuses; d and f find shorter sides. Every part directly applies Pythagoras’ theorem and basic surd results, supporting the selected primary and secondary skills.
questions.methodNote: Pages 1 and 3 illustrate Pythagoras’ theorem and square-root lengths. Page 3 gives square-root identities; page 4 teaches extracting perfect-square factors and exact surd form; page 5 reinforces surd operations. Complete prerequisite Pythagoras working, especially finding a shorter side, is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify hypotenuses and shorter sides, apply Pythagoras’ theorem and simplify exact square roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a square's area and use Pythagoras' theorem to obtain its diagonal in exact surd form.

questions.mappingNote: Part a squares the given side using the basic surd results. Part b identifies the diagonal as a hypotenuse, adds the squares of the two equal sides and simplifies the resulting square root. The primary skill is finding a side using Pythagoras' theorem; prerequisite-method acceptance remains unresolved.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes square-root results and illustrates Pythagoras' theorem through right-triangle constructions. Pages 4–5 demonstrate extracting perfect-square factors and retaining exact surd answers. The supplied evidence does not establish the square-area formula or a complete square-diagonal application of Pythagoras' theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a square's area and use Pythagoras' theorem to obtain its diagonal in exact surd form.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate an area with a surd measurement and use Pythagoras’ theorem to obtain and simplify an exact diagonal length.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies rectangle area to the given surd width. Part b applies Pythagoras’ theorem to the rectangle’s perpendicular sides, then simplifies the positive square root by extracting the factor 4. Original prerequisite method evidence remains required.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes squaring square roots and multiplying radicals; pages 4–5 demonstrate extracting perfect-square factors. Pages 1 and 3 illustrate Pythagoras’ theorem but do not establish full rectangle-diagonal working. Rectangle area prerequisite teaching is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate an area with a surd measurement and use Pythagoras’ theorem to obtain and simplify an exact diagonal length.

classification.difficultyReason: Retain the common radical and combine its signed coefficients; all terms are already like surds.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b add two positive coefficients; c and d combine signed coefficients; e and f combine three signed coefficients. Every radical is already simplified, so Example 8's preliminary simplification is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: The introduction identifies like surds as multiples of the same radical. Example 7 combines their coefficients while retaining the common radical.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two or three signed coefficients of already-like surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Group terms by radical and combine signed coefficients, then simplify the remaining square root of 8 in part f.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses addition and subtraction of surds; part f also requires simplifying sqrt(8).
questions.methodNote: Collect like surds as in Example 7; simplify square factors as in Examples 2, 3 and 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Collect coefficients of like surds, simplifying sqrt(8) in the final part.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine missing positive or negative surd expressions by comparing like terms.

questions.mappingNote: Example 7 supplies like-term arithmetic; the completion task applies its inverse.
questions.methodNote: Compare coefficients of like surds, using addition or subtraction to find the missing expression.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine missing positive or negative surd expressions by comparing like terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and incorporate outer coefficients before identifying and combining like surds, retaining unlike radicals separately.

questions.mappingNote: The printed Example 8 reference directly supports every part; pages 3–4 establish square-factor simplification.
questions.methodNote: Factor out perfect squares, then combine like surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extract square factors and combine like surds with integer coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify radicals before combining like terms, including a fractional coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Example 8 supports the complete task; the fractional coefficient in k uses the same like-term method.
questions.methodNote: Simplify each radical using a perfect-square factor and collect like terms, retaining exact fractional coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify radicals before combining like terms, including a fractional coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify four-term expressions containing two distinct radical types.

questions.mappingNote: The four-term mixed-radical expressions extend Example 8 without a new method.
questions.methodNote: Simplify square factors first, then combine coefficients of each radical separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify four-term expressions containing two distinct radical types.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify a surd difference and identify the radicand, including a negative result.

questions.mappingNote: The main assessment is surd simplification, followed by identifying the number under the root.
questions.methodNote: Simplify the difference as in Example 8 and compare square roots; squaring reverses the positive square root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify a surd difference and identify the radicand, including a negative result.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine exact surd perimeter and area calculations with Pythagoras to obtain each diagonal.

questions.mappingNote: Finding the diagonal is the most advanced directly assessed skill. Original prerequisite method evidence is still required for method acceptance.
questions.methodNote: Use P=2(l+w), A=lw and d²=l²+w², then simplify exact surds. The supplied pages establish surd arithmetic and illustrate Pythagoras, but do not establish the full prerequisite perimeter, area and diagonal methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine exact surd perimeter and area calculations with Pythagoras to obtain each diagonal.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of square roots, with square-factor simplification in three parts.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess multiplication and simplification of square-root surds.
questions.methodNote: Multiply radicands and extract perfect-square factors, following the basic square-root rules and Examples 2, 3 and 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of square roots, with square-factor simplification in three parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct quotient-rule applications, with one further square-factor simplification.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses division and simplification of square-root surds.
questions.methodNote: Divide radicands using the square-root quotient rule and then remove any perfect-square factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct quotient-rule applications, with one further square-factor simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply numerical coefficients with the appropriate sign and multiply radicands; the resulting radicals need no further extraction.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts assess multiplication of numerical multiples of surds.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 multiplies coefficients and radicands separately. Apply ordinary sign rules to negative coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply numerical coefficients and radicands, including negative factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide coefficients and radicands separately, reduce numerical factors and express the final reciprocal root appropriately; rationalisation is unnecessary.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is division of surd expressions, including fractional numerical coefficients.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 9: divide coefficients and radicands separately. Retain the reciprocal-square-root result in part f, as in the answer evidence; rationalisation is not required here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify fractional coefficients and surd quotients, including negative coefficients and a reciprocal square root.

classification.difficultyReason: Use equal square-root factors to obtain integers, including numerical and negative coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies equal square-root multiplication to obtain an integer.
questions.methodNote: Use the basic identity that the square of a positive square root is its radicand; multiply numerical coefficients and apply sign rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use equal square-root factors to obtain integers, including numerical and negative coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a matching radical to make an integer product and determine its coefficient from the target; part j also requires simplifying the supplied root of 8.

questions.mappingNote: Each completion requires a coefficient times the matching square root to produce the stated integer; part j additionally simplifies sqrt(8). This directly assesses surd operations.
questions.methodNote: Use the multiplication rule for surds and the identity sqrt(a) × sqrt(a) = a. Simplify square factors where necessary, as in Examples 9 and 10 on PDF page 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete products using matching square roots and numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Find missing surd factors, numerators and denominators, sometimes after collecting like surds.

questions.mappingNote: All ten completions directly assess surd multiplication or division; g–j also require collecting like surds. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are unsuitable.
questions.methodNote: Multiply or divide coefficients and radicands separately, simplify square roots, and collect like surds before finding a missing factor or fraction component.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find missing surd factors, numerators and denominators, sometimes after collecting like surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Respect operation order, multiply or divide surd terms, simplify square factors where needed and then combine the resulting like surds.

questions.mappingNote: Each of a–f assesses multiplication followed by combining like surds; g–j assess division followed by combining like surds. No supplied reuse candidate contains this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Multiply or divide coefficients and radicands, extract square factors, then combine like surds. Example 10a, b supplies multiplication and division methods; page 8 supplies collecting like surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine surd multiplication or division with addition and subtraction of like surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Square both the coefficient and radical factor, extending the same rule to symbolic a and b in the final part.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly apply the basic surd squaring result; part h generalises the same calculation symbolically.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives the square-root product and squaring rules. Page 10 Example 10c expands a square as two identical factors, multiplies the coefficients and radicals, then evaluates. Page 8 concerns combining like surds and introduces no additional step needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of squaring a surd product, followed by a symbolic generalisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply repeated multiplication or power rules, pairing root factors and retaining one radical for odd powers while also raising the coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Every part evaluates a positive integral power of a numerical surd using repeated multiplication and paired roots; surd-results is the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies the square-root square identity; page 10 Example 10d expands a cube as repeated multiplication, pairs square-root factors, and simplifies. Page 8 concerns collecting like surds and is not needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply repeated multiplication and the square-root square identity to numerical powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Distribute the outside surd across both terms, track signs and coefficients, and extract square factors from the resulting products.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts directly assess expansion of a single surd factor across a binomial, followed where necessary by simplification. The offered reuse candidates have different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Apply the distributive law as in Example 11 on PDF page 11; multiply coefficients and radicands, then extract perfect-square factors using the basic surd results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distribute a surd factor across two terms and simplify resulting square roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand all four binomial products with correct signs, simplify radical products and decide which resulting integer or surd terms can combine.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess expansion and simplification of surd binomials. The printed Example 12 reference matches the inspected teaching example. None of the supplied reuse candidates has this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Use the distributive law to multiply every term in the second bracket by each term in the first, simplify radical products, then collect like terms. Page 11 Example 12 supplies the directly assessed binomial method; pages 3, 8 and 10 establish radical simplification and like surds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand twelve surd binomial products, simplify radicals and collect like terms with signed coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute signed surds into products, quotients, powers and reciprocal expressions, retaining exact simplified answers.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess surd operations after substitution. Page 10 Example 10d supplies the exact cube used in parts e, f and g. Part g retains the teacher's first equivalent answer because rationalising denominators is not established by these inspected teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given surds, multiply or divide coefficients and radicands, simplify square factors, and evaluate powers by repeated multiplication as in Examples 9 and 10. Combine the resulting exact values using ordinary arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed surds into products, quotients, powers and reciprocal expressions, retaining exact simplified answers.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute binomial surd values, distribute coefficients and signs, and expand a product before simplifying.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e use substitution, distribution and collection of like surds; f expands two surd binomials, g multiplies that product by the separate factor square root of 3, and h takes the square root of the complete product. Expansion of surd binomials is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the given values, distribute coefficients and subtraction signs, and collect like surds as on page 8. Expand binomial products term by term as in Example 12 on page 11, then use the square-root rules on page 3. Page 10 establishes surd multiplication and simplest-form answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute binomial surd values, distribute coefficients and signs, and expand a product before simplifying.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply rectangle formulas and expand and simplify products and sums involving surds.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply surd multiplication and like-term collection within rectangle calculations. Parts c and d require the binomial expansion demonstrated on page 11, making expand-surd-expressions the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes square-root product rules; page 8 collects like surds; page 10 multiplies and simplifies surds; page 11 expands binomial products term by term. Original prerequisite evidence for rectangle area and perimeter formulas is absent from the supplied teaching pages.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply rectangle formulas and expand and simplify products and sums involving surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine expansion of squared surd binomials with Pythagoras’ theorem, perimeter and triangle area.

questions.mappingNote: Expansion and simplification of squared surd binomials is the most advanced directly assessed algebraic skill. Part a also requires finding a shorter side; parts b and c apply perimeter and triangle-area formulas. Prerequisite method compatibility remains unresolved pending original teaching evidence.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes basic square-root results and illustrates Pythagoras’ theorem in surd construction. Page 8 combines like surds after simplification. Page 10 multiplies and simplifies surds; page 11 expands binomial products by distribution. The supplied evidence does not establish the complete shorter-side Pythagoras method, perimeter formula or triangle-area method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine expansion of squared surd binomials with Pythagoras’ theorem, perimeter and triangle area.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply square perimeter and area formulas, then expand and simplify a squared surd binomial.

questions.mappingNote: Part a distributes 4 across the side-length expression. Part b uses the binomial multiplication method of Example 12, simplifies the surd product and combines like terms. Expansion of surd expressions is the most advanced directly assessed skill; prerequisite geometry method evidence remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies square-root identities, page 8 combines like surds, page 10 multiplies surds and evaluates their powers, and page 11 expands binomial products using the distributive law. The supplied evidence does not establish square perimeter and area formulas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square perimeter and area formulas, then expand and simplify a squared surd binomial.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply binomial-square identities, including coefficients and fractions, and simplify the resulting surds.

questions.mappingNote: All fourteen parts directly apply the binomial-square identities to surd expressions; m and n additionally require exact fraction arithmetic.
questions.methodNote: Use the displayed squared-sum and squared-difference identities, as demonstrated in Example 13, then apply the basic surd results and collect terms. The conflicting Example 14(b) is not used.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply binomial-square identities, including coefficients and fractions, and simplify the resulting surds.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the supplied difference-of-squares pattern, square each complete term including its coefficient, and subtract in the correct order.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts are conjugate products. Parts a–d use unit surd coefficients; e–j square coefficients as well as radicals; k–l also square fractional terms. No offered reuse candidate has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Use the displayed difference-of-squares identity, square each surd term, then subtract. Page 3 supplies the square-root results; page 15 Example 14(a) demonstrates the method, and page 16 repeats the identity. The conflicting Example 14(b) is not used as method evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise conjugate surd factors and evaluate differences of squares, including fractional terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply square area and expand squared surd binomials using special products.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts require squaring the given side length and applying the positive or negative binomial-square identity. Special products is the directly assessed advanced skill; square area is a prerequisite.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supplies square-root arithmetic. Example 13 on page 15 demonstrates binomial-square expansion followed by surd simplification; page 16 repeats the special-product identities. The supplied teaching pages do not establish the prerequisite square-area formula. The conflicting Example 14(b) is not used.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square area and expand squared surd binomials using special products.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute two surd expressions and apply conjugate products and binomial squares.

questions.mappingNote: Part a is a conjugate product; b combines like surds; c expands and adds two squares; d applies difference of squares to the given expressions.
questions.methodNote: Use the square-root rules, binomial-square identities and difference of squares. Example 13 demonstrates expanding surd squares; Example 14(a) demonstrates conjugate multiplication. The conflicting Example 14(b) is not used as method evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two surd expressions and apply conjugate products and binomial squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate triangle area and an exact hypotenuse from two perpendicular surd lengths.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses triangle area using two perpendicular surd lengths. Part b assesses finding the hypotenuse and simplifying its exact surd value; this is the most advanced directly assessed skill. Prerequisite method evidence remains incomplete.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 supports multiplying and squaring surds and introduces Pythagorean construction of surd lengths. Pages 15–16 present special-product identities. None supplies a triangle-area method or a complete worked Pythagoras calculation for this task. The contradictory Example 14(b) is excluded as method evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate triangle area and an exact hypotenuse from two perpendicular surd lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the side lengths into Pythagoras, perimeter and area calculations, using squared binomials and conjugate products to simplify exact results.

questions.mappingNote: Special products is the primary chapter skill: part a uses the squared-binomial identities and part c uses difference of squares. Pythagoras, perimeter and triangle area are supporting applications.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 gives basic surd results and introductory Pythagorean constructions; page 8 combines like surds; page 11 demonstrates distributive expansion; page 15 demonstrates squared binomials and difference of squares. The solutions use these special products to simplify the side calculations. Complete prerequisite teaching for Pythagoras, perimeter and triangle area is absent from the supplied evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply square identities and difference of squares to exact surd lengths in three triangle calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the denominator's radical as the rationalising factor, distribute it across binomial numerators where present and reduce common numerical factors.

questions.mappingNote: All fifteen parts have one-term surd denominators. Parts a–k use numerical or single-surd numerators; l–o additionally distribute the multiplying surd across two numerator terms.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 multiplies numerator and denominator by the denominator's surd factor, expands products and simplifies surds and numerical factors. Examples 16–17 and the summary provide further context; conjugates are unnecessary for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Single-term surd denominators progress from numerical numerators to two-term surd numerators requiring expansion and simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: Rationalise each fraction, simplify coefficients and then choose a common denominator to combine the terms with correct signs.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly apply Example 16. Parts a, b, e, f and h rationalise both simple fractions; c, d and g also simplify numerical coefficients in monomial surd denominators.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 multiplies numerator and denominator by the denominator's surd. Example 16 rationalises first, then combines fractions using a common denominator. Pages 10–11 establish surd multiplication and simplification; the special-product and conjugate methods on pages 15 and 18–19 are unnecessary here.
